claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating contains a mixture of FCC and BCC phases.
Controlled annealing can increase the coherency of FCC/BCC interfaces relative to the as-deposited state.
Dislocation climb is the dominant deformation mechanism under the proposed elevated-temperature sustained-loading conditions.
More-coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Annealing-induced improvement in interface coherency creates stronger barriers to dislocation motion.
More-coherent FCC/BCC interfaces impede dislocation climb during sustained loading.
Impeded dislocation climb reduces plastic flow during sustained loading.
The annealed coating will have a lower creep strain rate than the as-deposited coating.
The proposed mechanism operates under sustained high stress and elevated temperature when creep is predominantly governed by dislocation climb.
Annealed and as-deposited samples should be tested under identical sustained-stress and elevated-temperature creep conditions.
Interface coherency should be measured by electron microscopy alongside creep strain rate and overall plastic deformation rate.
Failure of coherency-enhanced samples to show a statistically significant creep-rate reduction would falsify the proposed coherency-mediated improvement.
Failure of annealing to increase interface coherency would itself falsify the causal hypothesis.
